exercises.title: Explaining how you'd check what's running slow right now
exercises.skillTag: DMVs vs. Catalog Views (SQL Server Diagnostic Terminology)
exercises.situation: A teammate who mostly writes application code asks you, casually, how you'd figure out what's currently running slow on a production SQL Server instance. Explain how you'd approach it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd check the DMVs to see what's running right now and look at whatever query seems slow.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Check the DMVs' names a category of more than a dozen system views without saying which one, what column actually separates a slow request from a normal one, or how you'd turn a session ID into the actual query text behind it. It also doesn't distinguish a DMV from a catalog view or a DMF, so a listener can't tell if this person actually knows the difference between 'what the database looks like' and 'what the database is doing right now' — or whether they're about to query the wrong kind of object entirely.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests directly, since that's a Dynamic Management View describing activity happening right now — not a catalog view like sys.tables or sys.columns, which only describe structure. I'd order by total_elapsed_time so the longest-running request surfaces first, and pull wait_type and wait_time for each one to see what it's actually stuck on rather than just how long it's been running. To see the real query text behind a session ID, I'd use CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) — that's a Dynamic Management Function, not a view, which is why it needs a handle passed into it instead of being queryable on its own. If nothing stands out in requests but people are reporting general slowness, I'd check sys.dm_os_wait_stats too, understanding it's a cumulative counter since the instance last restarted rather than a log — a huge number there over six months of uptime doesn't automatically mean something's actively wrong, so I'd clear it with DBCC SQLPERF before a specific test if I wanted a clean before-and-after read. Once I have a specific query and its dominant wait type, that's the actual starting point for digging into an execution plan — not before.

scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Query the Dynamic Management Views and Functions that expose current activity, then pull the real query text behind whatever stands out.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: sys.dm_exec_requests surfaces current activity ordered by total_elapsed_time, wait_type and wait_time show what's actually being waited on, and CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text turns a session ID into the real query.

scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Decide whether the evidence points to one specific session or a system-wide pattern, and choose the next diagnostic step accordingly.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: A single long-running session narrows straight to one query and its plan; no single culprit but a server-wide complaint means checking sys.dm_os_wait_stats for the dominant wait type instead.

scopeBreakdown.explanation: Finding the query and its wait type is the handoff into reading an execution plan — the DMV query itself doesn't fix anything, it just tells you honestly where to look next.

vocabulary.definition: A built-in system view, queried directly with SELECT, that exposes what SQL Server is doing right now rather than what the database's structure looks like.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the correct first place to look for current activity — querying a catalog view instead would only show you structure, not what's actually running.
vocabulary.example: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests, a DMV, to see everything currently executing on the instance.

vocabulary.definition: A system function, called with CROSS APPLY or OUTER APPLY against a handle from a DMV, rather than queried on its own.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Knowing a DMF needs a handle passed in — not queried standalone — is what lets you actually turn a session ID into real query text.
vocabulary.example: I'd use CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle), a DMF, to pull the query text behind that session.

vocabulary.definition: A built-in view exposing SQL Server's metadata — what tables, columns, and indexes exist — as queryable rows.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Confusing a catalog view with a DMV leads to querying the wrong kind of object entirely when the actual question is about current activity, not structure.
vocabulary.example: sys.tables is a catalog view describing structure; it won't tell you what's running right now.

vocabulary.definition: The DMV listing every currently executing request, one row per request, including its wait information and elapsed time.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the actual starting point for 'what's running slow right now' — ordering it by total_elapsed_time surfaces the longest-running request first.
vocabulary.example: I'd order sys.dm_exec_requests by total_elapsed_time descending to find the longest-running request.

vocabulary.definition: Columns (and the related sys.dm_os_wait_stats view) describing what a request is actually waiting on and for how long, rather than just how long it's been running.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A long-running request and a request stuck on a specific wait are different problems with different fixes; wait_type tells you which one you're looking at.
vocabulary.example: I'd pull wait_type alongside total_elapsed_time, since a request can run long for very different reasons.

vocabulary.definition: SQL Server's lightweight, persistent tracing and diagnostic-collection engine, capable of capturing detailed event data continuously rather than just at the moment you happen to query a DMV.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A DMV only shows a snapshot of right now; Extended Events can capture a problem that happens intermittently, between the moments you happen to be looking. This course's DMV-focused lessons cover the snapshot approach; Extended Events is a deeper, always-on diagnostic layer beyond that scope.
vocabulary.example: Since this issue only happens for a few seconds at a time, I'd set up an Extended Events session to actually capture it instead of relying on catching it in a DMV snapshot.

languageUpgrades.weak: I'd check the DMVs.
languageUpgrades.professional: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests for current activity, then CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text to see the real query behind whichever session stands out.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Names the actual object and the actual technique instead of a vague category.

languageUpgrades.weak: The server's just slow right now.
languageUpgrades.professional: I'd check sys.dm_os_wait_stats for the dominant wait type, after clearing the counters so the read reflects right now and not six months of uptime.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Turns a vague feeling into a specific, checkable measurement.

languageUpgrades.weak: I'll look at the query.
languageUpgrades.professional: I'd pull the query text with sys.dm_exec_sql_text against the sql_handle from the request, since the session ID alone doesn't tell you what it's actually running.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Explains the actual mechanism instead of treating 'look at the query' as self-explanatory.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: I'd just open Activity Monitor and see what's slow.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: I'd start the same way Activity Monitor does under the hood — querying sys.dm_exec_requests directly — so I can filter and sort it exactly how I need instead of relying on a fixed GUI view.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: The database is probably just busy.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: I'd check whether total_elapsed_time on any single request is actually unusual before assuming the whole instance is 'busy' in general.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: I don't know which table has that information.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: Activity information doesn't live in a table at all — it's exposed through Dynamic Management Views like sys.dm_exec_requests, which reflect what's happening right now rather than stored data.

exercises.title: Explaining why a database couldn't be restored to the moment before a bad DELETE
exercises.situation: A manager asks why a database that 'has backups' still lost 20 minutes of data when it had to be restored after an accidental DELETE. Explain what actually determines how close to the failure point you can recover.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It has backups, so it should be able to restore to right before the delete happened. Maybe the backup job didn't run.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This assumes 'has backups' automatically means point-in-time recovery, without checking the one setting that actually controls that — the recovery model. It jumps to blaming the backup job before ruling out the much more likely explanation: the database is in SIMPLE recovery, where point-in-time recovery was never possible regardless of whether every backup ran perfectly.
exercises.professionalResponse: The first thing I'd check isn't whether the backup job ran — it's the database's recovery model, with SELECT name, recovery_model_desc FROM sys.databases. If it's in SIMPLE recovery, the transaction log auto-truncates after every checkpoint, so there's no log backup chain to restore through — recovery is only possible to the point of the last full or differential backup, full stop, no matter how reliable the backup job is. If it's in FULL recovery instead, then point-in-time recovery to just before the DELETE should have been possible using a full backup plus the chain of log backups up to that moment, and the actual problem is more likely a gap in that chain — a missed log backup, or someone switching to BULK_LOGGED for a bulk load without realizing a minimally-logged operation inside that window blocks point-in-time restore through it. Either way, I'd explain this to the business in terms of acceptable data loss rather than blaming a job: if losing 20 minutes isn't acceptable going forward, that's a recovery model and backup frequency decision, not a 'fix the job' ticket. I'd recommend switching SIMPLE to FULL and starting a real log backup schedule, while being clear that doesn't retroactively give point-in-time recovery for anything before the next full backup.

scopeBreakdown.label: Situation
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: A database restore after data loss recovered less recent data than the business expected, despite backups existing.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: A database restored after an accidental DELETE lost 20 minutes of recent data despite having backups, and a manager wants to know why.

scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Confirm the database's actual recovery model before assuming the backup job is at fault.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Checking recovery_model_desc in sys.databases is the single fact that determines whether this was ever recoverable to that point at all.

scopeBreakdown.label: Observe
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Review whether a full backup plus an unbroken log backup chain existed up to the point of failure.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: If the model is FULL, the real question becomes whether the log backup chain had a gap — a missed backup, or an unnoticed BULK_LOGGED window.

scopeBreakdown.label: Plan & Perform
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Choose the fix based on the actual cause: a recovery model change, or repairing the log backup chain.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: SIMPLE means point-in-time recovery was never possible and the fix is a model change plus a log backup schedule; FULL means tracing and closing the actual chain gap.

scopeBreakdown.label: Evaluate
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Confirm the new setup by testing a restore to a specific point in time, and agree the acceptable-loss number explicitly with the business.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Testing an actual point-in-time restore proves the new configuration works, and translating the tradeoff into an explicit number keeps the business informed, not just reassured.

vocabulary.definition: The database-level setting (SIMPLE, FULL, or BULK_LOGGED) that determines what happens to the transaction log and what recovery is actually possible.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the single setting that determines whether point-in-time recovery was ever possible, before anyone investigates the backup job itself.
vocabulary.example: I'd check the recovery model first, since that determines whether point-in-time recovery was ever possible here.

vocabulary.definition: Restoring a database to an exact moment in time, using a full backup plus the chain of log backups up to that moment.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's only possible under FULL (or BULK_LOGGED outside minimally-logged windows) — SIMPLE recovery rules it out entirely, regardless of backup reliability.
vocabulary.example: Point-in-time recovery to just before the DELETE requires FULL recovery and an unbroken log backup chain.

vocabulary.definition: The file that records every transaction against a database, which recovery models control the retention and truncation behavior of.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Whether the log retains history or truncates automatically is exactly what separates SIMPLE from FULL recovery.
vocabulary.example: In SIMPLE recovery, the transaction log is automatically truncated after each checkpoint.

vocabulary.definition: A recovery model that behaves like FULL for ordinary transactions but minimally logs certain bulk operations, which blocks point-in-time restore through that specific window.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A shop that switches to BULK_LOGGED for a bulk load and forgets to switch back can unknowingly create a gap in point-in-time recoverability.
vocabulary.example: If a log backup's window contains a minimally-logged bulk operation under BULK_LOGGED, you can only recover to the end of that backup, not a point inside it.

vocabulary.definition: The internal SQL Server process that periodically writes dirty (modified) pages from memory to disk, after which SIMPLE recovery can safely truncate log records no longer needed for crash recovery.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the actual mechanism that makes SIMPLE recovery's log truncation happen automatically; this recovery-model lesson names checkpoints as the trigger without going deep into how the checkpoint process itself works internally — that's SQLOS-level territory beyond this lesson's scope.
vocabulary.example: The log doesn't truncate continuously — it truncates after a checkpoint confirms those transactions are no longer needed for crash recovery.

vocabulary.definition: A formal planning metric stating the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as a span of time, agreed with the business ahead of any incident.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Translating '20 minutes was too much data loss' into an explicit RPO is what turns this conversation into a real requirement instead of a one-off complaint. This general administration course covers recovery models themselves; RPO as a formal metric is this path's HA/DR course territory, built directly on top of what recovery models make possible.
vocabulary.example: If 20 minutes of loss is unacceptable going forward, I'd ask the business to state an actual RPO so the backup strategy can be sized to meet it.

languageUpgrades.weak: It has backups, so it should have been fine.
languageUpgrades.professional: I'd check the recovery model first — SIMPLE recovery rules out point-in-time recovery entirely, regardless of how reliable the backup job is.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Replaces an assumption with the one setting that actually determines what was recoverable.

languageUpgrades.weak: The backup job probably failed.
languageUpgrades.professional: I'd rule out the recovery model before assuming the job failed, since a correctly-running job under SIMPLE recovery would still produce exactly this result.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Avoids blaming a process before checking the configuration that could fully explain the outcome on its own.

languageUpgrades.weak: We'll just make sure backups run more often.
languageUpgrades.professional: If the database is in SIMPLE recovery, running full backups more often still doesn't give point-in-time recovery — that requires switching to FULL recovery and adding log backups.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Names the actual fix instead of a plausible-sounding one that wouldn't solve the real problem.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: I think the backups are broken somehow.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: Before assuming the backups are broken, I'd confirm the recovery model, since SIMPLE recovery alone fully explains this outcome with a perfectly working backup job.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: We should just back up more often so this doesn't happen.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: More frequent full backups don't give point-in-time recovery on their own — that specifically requires FULL recovery plus a log backup chain.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: I'll tell them it's fixed now.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: I'd confirm the fix with an actual test restore to a specific point in time before telling anyone point-in-time recovery is now in place.

Did you correctly explain what SIMPLE recovery does and doesn't allow?
Did you distinguish FULL recovery's log backup chain from a single full backup?
Did you reframe the issue as an acceptable-data-loss decision for the business, not just a technical fix?
Did you describe how you'd actually verify the fix with a test restore?

exercises.title: Explaining why adding an index didn't fix a slow report
exercises.situation: You added an index that matches a report's WHERE clause exactly, but the report is still slow. Explain to another developer what's likely still happening and what term describes the fix.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I added the right index already, so I'm not sure why it's still slow. Maybe it needs a different index.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'The right index' isn't actually defined — an index that matches the WHERE clause's filter column can still force an expensive extra step for every row if it doesn't also hold every other column the query needs. This answer has no execution-plan evidence and no name for the actual mechanism, so it can't explain what's different about the index that would fix it.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd pull up the actual execution plan first, because 'the right index' for a WHERE clause and a covering index for the whole query are two different things. If the index only has CustomerId as a key column but the SELECT list also needs OrderDate and TotalDue, the plan will show an Index Seek on CustomerId feeding into a Key Lookup back to the clustered index for those other columns — joined by a Nested Loops operator, one lookup per matching row. For a handful of rows that's invisible; for a report scanning thousands of customers, the Key Lookups can dominate the plan's total cost far more than the seek itself did. The actual fix is to make the index covering — adding OrderDate and TotalDue as INCLUDE columns so every column the query needs is available directly from the nonclustered index, which removes the Key Lookup and the Nested Loops join entirely. I'd weigh that against the tradeoff before widening it, though: every included column makes the index bigger on disk and adds write cost to every INSERT or UPDATE that touches those columns, so I'd only do this for a query that runs often enough to be worth that ongoing cost — not a report that runs once a month.

scopeBreakdown.label: Situation
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: An index matching a query's filter column didn't resolve its performance problem.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: An index was added matching the report's WHERE clause exactly, but the report is still slow, and a colleague wants to know why.

scopeBreakdown.label: Clarify
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Confirm what 'the right index' actually means for this specific query before assuming a different index is needed.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: An index matching the filter column and a covering index for the whole query are different things — that distinction has to be checked before changing anything.

scopeBreakdown.label: Observe
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Read the execution plan for the specific operators — Index Seek, Key Lookup, Nested Loops — that reveal what's actually costing time.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: A Key Lookup fed by Nested Loops after an Index Seek is the visible signature of a non-covering index, and its cost scales with row count.

scopeBreakdown.label: Plan & Perform
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Widen the index to cover the query's full column list, weighing the write-cost tradeoff against how often the query actually runs.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Adding OrderDate and TotalDue as INCLUDE columns removes the Key Lookup entirely, but only makes sense for a query run often enough to justify the added write cost.

scopeBreakdown.label: Evaluate
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Confirm in the plan that the Key Lookup and its join are gone after the change.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Re-checking the plan after widening the index confirms the fix actually removed the Key Lookup, rather than assuming it worked because the index now 'matches' more columns.

whatMakesThisSoundSenior.howThisResponseShowsIt: Names the exact plan operators — Index Seek, Key Lookup, Nested Loops — and the exact fix — a covering index with INCLUDE columns — instead of 'a different index.'

whatMakesThisSoundSenior.description: Explains a logical investigation and decision-making process.
whatMakesThisSoundSenior.howThisResponseShowsIt: Starts from the execution plan as evidence, explains the mechanism causing the cost, and only then proposes the specific fix.

whatMakesThisSoundSenior.description: Connects technical problems to business impact.
whatMakesThisSoundSenior.howThisResponseShowsIt: Frames the fix's cost in terms of how often the report actually runs, not as a universally 'better' index to apply everywhere.

whatMakesThisSoundSenior.description: Considers evidence, risks, alternatives, and tradeoffs before recommending solutions.
whatMakesThisSoundSenior.howThisResponseShowsIt: Explicitly weighs the write-cost tradeoff of a wider index before recommending it, rather than treating 'add more columns' as free.

whatMakesThisSoundSenior.description: Explains how success would be measured and verified.
whatMakesThisSoundSenior.howThisResponseShowsIt: States that confirming the fix means re-checking the plan for the Key Lookup's absence, not just assuming the wider index worked.

vocabulary.definition: An index that contains every column a specific query needs, so the query never has to touch the clustered index at all.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the actual fix for a Key Lookup problem — an index matching only the WHERE clause isn't automatically covering.
vocabulary.example: I'd make this index covering by adding OrderDate and TotalDue as INCLUDE columns.

vocabulary.definition: The execution plan operator representing a trip back to the clustered index to fetch columns a nonclustered index doesn't hold.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Spotting a Key Lookup in a plan is what reveals that an index isn't covering, even when it correctly matches the filter.
vocabulary.example: The plan shows an Index Seek feeding a Key Lookup — that's the signature of a non-covering index.

vocabulary.definition: A column stored in a nonclustered index's leaf level without being part of the index key, added specifically to make an index covering.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Included columns are the mechanism for covering a query without changing how the index is actually seeked on.
vocabulary.example: I'd add OrderDate and TotalDue as included columns rather than key columns, since they're not filtered on.

vocabulary.definition: The join operator typically pairing an Index Seek with its per-row Key Lookup, running the lookup once for every row the seek returns.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Its cost scales directly with row count, which is why a Key Lookup is invisible for a handful of rows but dominant for a large report.
vocabulary.example: The Nested Loops operator runs the Key Lookup once per matching row, which adds up fast on a large report.

vocabulary.definition: The added write cost to INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operations that comes from maintaining a wider covering index.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the real cost side of the covering-index tradeoff — widening an index isn't free, it's a deliberate tradeoff against write performance.
vocabulary.example: I'd weigh the write amplification from widening this index against how often the report actually runs.

vocabulary.definition: SQL Server's built-in suggestions (via sys.dm_db_missing_index_* views) for indexes that might help a workload, generated from query patterns the optimizer has seen.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: These suggestions don't account for write cost, column order quality, or whether the query is worth covering at all — a real professional nuance beyond just reading the suggestion as an instruction, since blindly applying every suggested index is a common way to accumulate unnecessary write overhead.
vocabulary.example: The missing index DMVs suggested this column, but I'd still check the actual query frequency and write cost before creating it.

languageUpgrades.weak: I added the right index already.
languageUpgrades.professional: I added an index matching the WHERE clause, but I'd check the execution plan for a Key Lookup before assuming it's actually covering the query.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Distinguishes matching the filter from covering the whole query, with a specific way to check.

languageUpgrades.weak: Maybe it needs a different index.
languageUpgrades.professional: I'd widen the existing index with INCLUDE columns for OrderDate and TotalDue, rather than guessing at a different index entirely.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Names a specific, targeted change instead of an undefined 'different' index.

languageUpgrades.weak: More indexes should make it faster.
languageUpgrades.professional: I'd only add included columns to this index if the query runs often enough to be worth the extra write cost on every insert and update.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Replaces a blanket assumption with an explicit cost-benefit check.

sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: I'd check the plan for a Key Lookup — the index can be technically correct for the filter and still not be covering the whole query.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: Let's just add indexes on everything this query touches.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: I'd only widen the index to cover columns this specific query actually needs, since every extra included column adds ongoing write cost.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: It's fast enough now, I think.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: I'd confirm in the plan that the Key Lookup and its Nested Loops join are actually gone, not just assume the change helped.

exercises.title: Explaining '99.99% uptime, and we can't lose any data' to a DBA team
exercises.situation: A stakeholder says the new order-processing database needs '99.99% uptime, and we can't lose any data.' Explain how you'd translate that into something your team can actually design around.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Okay, we'll set up Always On so it's basically always up and we won't lose data.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Basically always up' isn't a number, and 'won't lose data' isn't a number either — both halves of the stakeholder's request need to become explicit, checkable figures before any technology gets chosen. This answer also treats Always On as a single blanket solution without checking whether its configuration (synchronous vs. asynchronous) actually matches what 'no data loss' requires.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd translate both halves of that statement into actual numbers before picking anything. exercises.title: Explaining why a MongoDB-backed feature sometimes shows slightly stale data
exercises.situation: A product manager asks why a new MongoDB-backed feature sometimes shows slightly stale data instead of just 'always showing the right answer, all the time.' Explain the real constraint behind that tradeoff.
exercises.beginnerResponse: MongoDB just isn't as strict as SQL Server about data being correct. We could probably turn that off if we wanted it to always be accurate.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This frames a deliberate, well-understood distributed-systems tradeoff as a MongoDB shortcoming you could simply 'turn off,' which isn't accurate and would lead to proposing a change that either doesn't exist or breaks availability. It doesn't name the actual theorem that makes this a real engineering constraint rather than a product of MongoDB being 'less strict.'
exercises.professionalResponse: This isn't MongoDB cutting corners — it's the CAP theorem, which applies to any distributed system, including a multi-region SQL Server Always On setup. During a network partition, a distributed system can't guarantee both Consistency — every read gets the absolute latest write — and Availability — every request gets a response — at the same time; it has to lean one way. MongoDB defaults toward consistency within a single replica set, since all writes go through one primary, but reads can be configured toward availability using eventual-consistency read concerns, which is almost certainly what's producing the slightly-stale reads here. That's the BASE model — Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency — a deliberate alternative to strict ACID consistency, appropriate for a feature where a response that's a second or two stale is a much better outcome than a response that fails outright. Before proposing any change, I'd confirm which read concern the application is actually using, and I'd frame the real decision for the product manager as a tradeoff, not a bug: tightening consistency is possible, but it means some reads will wait longer or fail during a network issue instead of returning a slightly old answer — which might be the wrong tradeoff for a feature like this one.

exercises.title: A nightly batch job is grinding to a halt and three other jobs are stuck behind it
exercises.situation: Multiple overnight jobs are reporting as 'still running' well past when they normally finish, and nobody can tell which one is actually the problem. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd check if something is blocking something else and kill whatever's blocking it.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Something is blocking something else' doesn't name a query, a DMV, or a method for finding the actual blocker — and jumping straight to 'kill it' skips verifying that the session you'd kill is actually the root cause rather than just another link in the chain. Killing the wrong session in the middle of a multi-session chain does nothing, because its own blocker is still blocked upstream.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests filtered to blocking_session_id <> 0, which lists every session currently blocked and exactly which session_id is blocking it. Since overnight jobs can block each other several sessions deep, I wouldn't stop at the first link — I'd walk the chain recursively, following blocking_session_id back until I reach a session that isn't itself being blocked by anything. That root session is usually not blocked at all; it's just running a long operation — an unindexed scan inside an explicit transaction, or a big update — that's holding locks everyone downstream needs. I'd pull its actual query text with CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(sql_handle) and check wait_resource to see exactly what object it's holding, before deciding anything. Only once I've confirmed that session is genuinely the root — not just killing whichever session happens to be reported as blocking the job someone complained about — would I decide whether to let it finish, or kill it and accept whatever rollback and reprocessing cost that creates for the batch it belongs to.

exercises.situation: A stored procedure runs in under a second for nearly every customer, but takes 40 seconds for one specific large customer. Statistics were updated yesterday. Explain how you'd confirm the cause.
exercises.beginnerResponse: The statistics are probably out of date, so I'd update them again just to be safe.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Statistics were already confirmed updated yesterday, so re-updating them isn't a diagnosis, it's a guess that ignores the evidence already given. This also treats stale statistics as the default explanation for any estimated-vs-actual mismatch, without running the one test that actually distinguishes stale statistics from parameter sniffing.
exercises.professionalResponse: Since statistics are already current, I'd treat stale statistics as ruled out and run the actual decisive test for parameter sniffing: OPTION (RECOMPILE) on this specific call, forcing a fresh compile using this customer's actual parameter value instead of reusing whatever plan is sitting in the cache. If the recompiled plan is dramatically better for this customer, that confirms it's parameter sniffing — the cached plan was built the first time the procedure ran, almost certainly for a typical small customer with few orders, and a Nested Loops plan that's cheap for five orders performs terribly for this customer's 12,000. Once that's confirmed, I'd pick the fix based on how often this happens: OPTION (RECOMPILE) on every call if this procedure runs infrequently enough that paying compile cost every time is cheap relative to execution; OPTIMIZE FOR a specific representative value, or OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, if I want one stable plan without per-call recompilation; or, if we're on SQL Server 2022 or Azure SQL Database under the newer compatibility level, letting Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization cache multiple plan variants automatically, since that addresses exactly this skewed-distribution problem without a query rewrite. I'd validate whichever fix I pick by re-running this customer's call and a handful of typical small-customer calls afterward, confirming both are fast — not just the one everybody complained about.

exercises.title: A secondary replica shows 'Not Synchronizing' and nobody's sure if failover still works
exercises.situation: One of the two secondary replicas in an Always On Availability Group has been showing a 'Not Synchronizing' state for an unknown amount of time. Explain how you'd investigate, and what you'd check before anyone assumes failover is safe.

exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Restarting without first checking why synchronization stopped skips the diagnosis entirely, and 'not synchronizing' can mean several very different things — a broken network path, a full transaction log on the primary unable to send data, or a replica that was manually suspended — each needing a different fix. A restart might mask the symptom temporarily without addressing the actual cause, and it does nothing to tell anyone whether failover is currently safe to rely on.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by checking the actual synchronization state and health through sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states and the Always On dashboard, rather than restarting anything first — 'Not Synchronizing' specifically, distinct from 'Synchronizing' or 'Synchronized,' usually means replication has stopped entirely rather than just lagging. I'd check whether someone manually suspended data movement on that replica, whether there's a network connectivity issue between the primary and that specific secondary, and whether the primary's transaction log is growing because it can't confirm the secondary has hardened the data — all three produce this same visible symptom for different reasons. If this replica matters for automatic failover specifically, I'd also treat this as urgent regardless of root cause, because an AG with a non-synchronizing secondary isn't actually providing the failover protection anyone assumes it is — if the primary failed right now, that replica either isn't a viable failover target or would come up with stale, incomplete data. I'd fix the actual cause — resume data movement if it was suspended, resolve the network path, or address the log growth — and then confirm the fix by checking the synchronization state return to 'Synchronized' and the redo queue actually draining, not just that the dashboard icon turned green once.

exercises.title: A nightly index maintenance job failed and the T-SQL looks correct
exercises.situation: A SQL Server Agent job that's run successfully for months failed last night. The T-SQL inside the failing step hasn't changed. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd look at the stored procedure the job runs and check the T-SQL for errors.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This jumps straight to reviewing code that was already stated as unchanged, skipping the actual first move — reading the job's own history, which records exactly which step failed and the real error message SQL Server already captured. It also assumes the failure must be a T-SQL logic problem, missing the much more common real-world cause for an otherwise-correct job that suddenly fails: a permissions or environment issue in the step's execution context, not the SQL itself.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before touching the stored procedure at all, I'd query msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory joined to sysjobs for this specific job, ordered by run_date and run_time descending — that history records which step_id actually failed and, in the message column, the verbatim error SQL Server already captured, whether that's a T-SQL error, an OS-level error for a CmdExec step, or a PowerShell exception. If the job has multiple steps, I wouldn't assume it's the T-SQL step specifically — a five-step job commonly fails on step three while the first two succeed cleanly, so I'd isolate the exact step_id before looking anywhere else. Given that the T-SQL itself hasn't changed, the most common real cause I'd check is the Agent service account's permissions: a CmdExec or PowerShell step runs as the SQL Server Agent service account by default, not as my own login, and I'd check sp_help_jobstep for that step to see whether a proxy account is configured or whether it's running under the bare service account — something like an expiring credential or a changed network share permission can break a step that's technically unchanged. I'd also rule out a schedule conflict with another maintenance job and a dependent resource — a linked server or file share — not being available yet at the time this job runs, since both can produce an identical-looking failure on correct T-SQL. Once I've confirmed the actual cause, I'd fix the underlying permission or dependency issue rather than just rerunning the job and hoping, and validate by letting it run on its normal schedule and confirming sysjobhistory shows a clean success, not just a manual one-off run.

exercises.title: A PostgreSQL table is growing and queries against it keep getting slower
exercises.situation: A heavily-updated PostgreSQL orders table has been getting progressively slower to query for weeks, and its on-disk size keeps growing even though the actual row count is roughly flat. Explain how you'd investigate, especially for someone coming from a SQL Server background.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd probably just rebuild the indexes, like I would on SQL Server when things get slow.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This reaches for a SQL Server fix — index rebuilds for fragmentation — without checking whether the actual PostgreSQL-specific mechanism even applies here. SQL Server's locking-based concurrency doesn't create the problem this symptom usually describes, so an index rebuild might not touch the real cause at all, and this answer shows no awareness that PostgreSQL has a genuinely different reason tables grow under heavy updates.
exercises.professionalResponse: This looks like table bloat, and the mechanism behind it doesn't exist in SQL Server, so I wouldn't reach for a SQL Server fix first. PostgreSQL uses MVCC — instead of locking a row to update it, an UPDATE writes a new row version and marks the old one as no longer current, and a DELETE marks a row as invisible rather than erasing it immediately. Both leave a dead tuple: a row version nobody's transaction can see anymore, but which still physically occupies space. I'd confirm this with SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables — if n_dead_tup is climbing steadily while n_live_tup stays roughly flat, that's the signature of bloat outrunning cleanup. Normally PostgreSQL's autovacuum daemon reclaims dead tuple space automatically once a table crosses a threshold, so I'd check whether autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor and autovacuum_vacuum_threshold are tuned too conservatively for this table's actual write volume, or whether a long-running transaction elsewhere is holding back what VACUUM can consider truly dead. If autovacuum is genuinely falling behind, I'd run a manual VACUUM ANALYZE to reclaim space for reuse and refresh planner statistics at the same time — and only reach for VACUUM FULL, which rewrites the whole table and requires an exclusive lock, as a deliberate, scheduled maintenance action, not a casual fix, since it blocks all reads and writes on the table for its duration. I'd validate by re-checking n_dead_tup after a reasonable window and confirming query times against this table actually improve, not just that the vacuum command completed.

exercises.title: Deciding where a legacy on-prem SQL Server database should land in Azure
exercises.situation: A team wants to move an on-prem SQL Server database to Azure. It uses SQL Server Agent jobs, linked servers, and cross-database queries. Explain how you'd decide which Azure SQL option to recommend.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We should just use Azure SQL Database since that's the main Azure SQL product.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This defaults to the most commonly-mentioned option without checking it against the workload's actual requirements, and it ignores every detail given in the scenario — Agent jobs and cross-database queries are specifically things Azure SQL Database's database-scoped model doesn't support, which this recommendation would discover only after migration started failing.
exercises.professionalResponse: I wouldn't default to Azure SQL Database here, because the workload's actual requirements rule it out before cost or convenience even enter the conversation. Azure SQL Database is database-scoped PaaS — no instance-level surface, no traditional SQL Server Agent, no cross-database queries by default — so a workload that depends on Agent jobs and cross-database queries wouldn't just need rework, it would lose capabilities Azure SQL Database structurally doesn't offer. Azure SQL Managed Instance is the right fit instead: it's still PaaS, so Microsoft still handles patching, backups, and the underlying OS, but it gives you an actual instance — SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries, linked servers, CLR — which is precisely why Managed Instance exists as a separate product rather than a bigger tier of Azure SQL Database. The real tradeoff I'd flag going in is deployment time and a hard networking requirement: Managed Instance needs a dedicated subnet inside a VNet, which is more setup than Azure SQL Database's near-instant provisioning. I'd only recommend SQL Server on an Azure VM instead if there were something here Managed Instance genuinely can't do either — OS-level access, an unsupported feature, or a third-party agent that has to run alongside SQL Server — because that option hands back the patching and backup responsibility Managed Instance and Azure SQL Database both take off a DBA's plate.

exercises.title: Deciding between Failover Cluster Instances and Availability Groups for a new SQL Server deployment
exercises.situation: A team is standing up a new on-prem SQL Server environment and asks whether they should use a Failover Cluster Instance or an Availability Group for high availability. Explain how you'd make that recommendation.
exercises.beginnerResponse: AG is newer, so we should just use that.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Newer' isn't a technical reason, and it skips checking what each technology actually protects against, what each one requires, and what this specific environment's storage and licensing situation looks like. FCI and AG protect against different failure modes — recommending one over the other without naming that difference means the recommendation isn't actually grounded in this environment's real constraints.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start with what each one actually protects against, because they're not interchangeable upgrades of each other. FCI protects against a node failure — if the server or OS dies, another node picks up the same instance on the same shared storage — but it doesn't protect against the shared storage itself failing, since there's only ever one copy of the data. AG protects at the database level by replicating to independent storage on separate replicas, which covers the storage-failure case FCI can't, but each replica needs its own full storage footprint, and features like readable secondaries bring licensing and edition considerations into the decision that a single-instance FCI doesn't require. So the real question isn't which one is newer, it's: does this environment already have reliable shared storage, and is losing that storage an acceptable residual risk? If they have a solid SAN and want node-level protection without doubling storage, FCI is a legitimate, still-current choice. If storage-level failure is a real concern, or they want per-database granularity, AG is the better fit. I'd also flag the honest real-world answer many production environments land on: combining both, running SQL Server as an FCI at each site for cheap node-level protection, then an AG between sites for storage and geographic protection — which isn't a compromise, it's a deliberate layered design once the budget and requirements support it.

exercises.title: Designing a deployment pipeline for database schema changes
exercises.situation: A development team wants database schema changes to go through the same automated pipeline their application code already uses. Explain how you'd architect that for a database specifically, rather than just copying the app pipeline.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We'll just add the database scripts to the same pipeline the app uses and have it run them automatically all the way to production.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats a database deployment as identical in risk profile to a stateless app deployment, proposing full automatic production deployment without acknowledging that a bad database change is far harder to fully undo than a bad app deployment. It also doesn't separate what CI validates from what CD actually deploys, so there's no clear description of what happens at each stage or where a human checkpoint belongs.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd architect this with CI and CD doing genuinely different jobs, and a deliberate human gate at the step that matters most. On every pull request, CI builds the database project — the .sqlproj — which parses every object script and fails the build if anything's internally inconsistent, like a view referencing a column that no longer exists; that step validates the change but deploys nothing anywhere. Once a change passes CI and is merged, I'd have it deploy automatically to a test or staging environment and run automated tests against that environment — this is the continuous deployment half for non-production. For production specifically, though, I'd choose continuous delivery rather than full continuous deployment: the pipeline builds, validates, and gets the change ready to go, but a human still clicks the final approval, because a bad database change is much harder to fully roll back than a bad stateless app deployment — a schema change that's already run against live data isn't something you can just redeploy the previous container image to undo. I'd make sure the review gate from source control (pull request review before merge) stays the actual technical checkpoint, with CI/CD automating everything mechanical that happens after that review — removing the easy-to-forget manual steps between 'this was approved' and 'this is actually running,' not replacing the review itself.

exercises.title: Designing a sharded MongoDB cluster that doesn't funnel all its writes through one shard
exercises.situation: A collection is growing past what one MongoDB server can hold, and the team wants to shard it. Explain how you'd approach choosing a shard key, and why that choice matters so much.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We'll just shard it on the _id field since that's always there on every document.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This picks the shard key for convenience — it's always present — without checking the two properties that actually determine whether sharding on that field will work. _id in MongoDB is typically a monotonically increasing ObjectId, which is exactly the kind of key that creates a write hotspot instead of actually distributing load.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd check two properties of any candidate shard key before picking one, because the shard key is chosen once, up front, and is genuinely difficult to change afterward. First, cardinality — a key with only a handful of distinct values can only ever split into a few chunks, capping how far the data can spread no matter how many shards exist. Second, and more relevant to the _id suggestion here: whether the key is monotonically increasing. MongoDB's default _id is an ObjectId that increases over time, so sharding on it means every new document's key value is higher than the last — all new writes land on whichever shard owns the current highest range, until it splits, which is the exact same hotspot problem a relational DBA already recognizes from a bad monotonic partition key. I'd look instead for a field with naturally high cardinality and a distribution that spreads writes evenly across the key's range — or, if nothing natural fits that well, a hashed version of a candidate key specifically to break up a monotonic pattern. I'd also confirm the application's actual query patterns against the candidate key, since mongos — the query router — can only target a single shard efficiently when a query includes the shard key; a key chosen purely for write distribution but never present in the application's real queries would force expensive cross-shard fan-out reads, trading one performance problem for another.

exercises.title: Scoping a SQL Server to PostgreSQL migration before committing to a timeline
exercises.situation: Leadership wants a firm timeline for migrating a SQL Server database to PostgreSQL. Explain how you'd approach producing that estimate responsibly, rather than just extrapolating from the table count.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We have about 400 tables, so based on similar projects I'd guess this takes around three months.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: A table count alone says nothing about what's actually hard in a cross-platform migration — stored procedures, triggers, linked servers, and application-embedded SQL don't show up in a table count at all, and this estimate has no inventory, no dependency check, and no accounting for SQL Server features PostgreSQL simply doesn't have. A guess extrapolated from a different project's table count is exactly the kind of estimate that turns out wrong by two or three times.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before giving any timeline, I'd build a real inventory first — not just tables, but views, stored procedures, functions, triggers, SQL Agent jobs, linked servers, and every login and permission grant, pulled directly from sys.objects, sys.tables, and sys.sql_modules rather than from documentation, since undocumented objects are exactly the ones that break a migration late. A database with 40 tables and 300 stored procedures is a fundamentally different project than one with 400 tables and 30 procedures, even though both look like '500 objects' in a simple count. From there I'd map dependencies the inventory alone won't show: linked servers, which PostgreSQL has no drop-in replacement for and would need postgres_fdw or dblink instead; cross-database queries, which are trivial in SQL Server and often impossible in the same form on the target; and application-embedded SQL — hardcoded T-SQL inside the application or ORM-generated SQL Server-specific syntax — which never shows up in a database-only inventory and is often the single largest source of rework. I'd also do a deliberate pass looking for features with no PostgreSQL equivalent — Service Broker, CLR integration, specific FILESTREAM usage — during assessment, not six weeks into development, since some of those mean a redesign and some mean a piece has to stay on SQL Server permanently. Only with all of that in hand would I build a timeline that estimates schema conversion, code conversion, data movement, application changes, testing, and a cutover period separately, with an explicit contingency that scales with how much application-embedded SQL was found — and I'd be upfront with leadership that a credible number comes after this assessment, not before it.

exercises.title: Deciding whether to escalate a production issue you haven't solved yet
exercises.situation: You've been working a production database issue for 45 minutes with no resolution, and it's starting to affect more than one application. Explain how you'd decide whether to escalate, and what you'd actually say.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd keep trying to fix it myself since escalating might make it look like I can't handle it, and I'd tell people it'll probably be fixed soon.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats escalating as a personal failure rather than a normal part of incident response, which is backwards — escalating too late after struggling silently costs real time everyone else could have used, while escalating early on a genuinely large incident costs almost nothing. It also proposes giving a guessed ETA, which is a specific, named mistake: a DBA who says 'fixed soon' and misses that badly damages trust more than one who honestly says the ETA isn't known yet.
exercises.professionalResponse: Two honest signals tell me it's time to escalate here, not one guess: I've already spent a reasonable amount of time without stabilizing it, and the blast radius has grown beyond one application to several — that's bigger than something to handle alone under time pressure. I'd escalate to the senior DBA or broader DBA team if this still looks technically beyond what I've been able to diagnose in 45 minutes, and separately flag it to the application teams if anything suggests this is actually rooted in how an app is using the database rather than the database itself. For the status update itself, I'd keep it to the same small, honest shape regardless of audience: impact in terms non-DBAs understand — which applications are actually affected, not which stored procedure is blocked — what's being done right now, and an ETA only if I genuinely have one. If I don't have a real ETA yet, I'd say exactly that — 'still assessing, next update in 15 minutes' — rather than guessing a number, because a wrong guess repeated to other people damages trust far more than an honest 'I don't know yet' does. I'd rather escalate and be told I had it handled than stay quiet past the point where someone with more context or authority could have helped.

exercises.title: Keeping technical recovery and stakeholder updates from colliding during a declared disaster
exercises.situation: During a declared disaster recovery event, the DBA actually performing the Availability Group failover is also personally fielding messages from five different stakeholders asking for updates. Explain what's wrong with that setup and what you'd change.
exercises.beginnerResponse: They should just answer the messages quickly between steps so people aren't left waiting.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This accepts the current structure and just asks for faster multitasking, which doesn't fix the actual problem — the same person doing failover and fielding five simultaneous stakeholders means both jobs suffer, because attention split during a technical failover is exactly when mistakes happen, and rushed answers to stakeholders are worse answers. The fix here is structural, not a request for the DBA to work faster.
exercises.professionalResponse: The real problem isn't speed, it's that the same person is doing two jobs that actively interfere with each other at the worst possible moment. During a disaster, the volume of people wanting information is much larger than a routine incident — leadership, other IT teams, sometimes customers — and figuring out who talks to whom live, under pressure, wastes time the recovery itself needs. I'd fix this structurally: designate a separate communication role, decided as part of the DR plan before any disaster happens, not improvised during one — someone who gets updates from the recovery team on a set cadence and translates that into what each stakeholder audience actually needs, freeing the DBA doing the failover to just do the failover. I'd keep the actual status updates to the same honest shape as a routine incident — impact, current action, and an ETA only when it's genuinely known — but acknowledge the stakes are higher at disaster scale: something like 'we're executing the failover runbook for the customer database, expect service partially restored within 30 minutes, next update at [time]' is honest and useful, while a guessed ETA repeated to leadership and possibly customers damages trust at a scale a missed internal ETA never would. A DR plan with excellent technical runbooks but no defined communication role still produces chaos during a real event, which is exactly the gap here.

exercises.title: Turning 'we can't afford much downtime or data loss' into an actual technical plan
exercises.situation: A stakeholder says the new order-processing database 'can't lose more than a few minutes of data, and needs to be back within 30 minutes if it goes down during business hours.' Explain how you'd turn that into a concrete recommendation.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We'll set up good backups and Always On and that should cover it.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Good backups and Always On' doesn't convert the stakeholder's actual numbers into a specific requirement — it names technology before translating the business statement into RPO and RTO figures, which skips the step that determines whether 'good backups' is anywhere close to sufficient, or whether Always On needs to be configured synchronously versus asynchronously to actually meet what was asked for.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd convert that sentence into explicit numbers before naming any technology: 'can't lose more than a few minutes' becomes an RPO of around 5 minutes, and 'back within 30 minutes' becomes an RTO of 30 minutes. That RPO already rules out nightly-only backups outright, since a nightly backup alone gives roughly a 24-hour RPO regardless of how reliable the backup job is — it requires log backups or replication running at least every 5 minutes. The RTO rules out a manual restore-from-tape process as the primary recovery mechanism, since someone getting paged, locating backups, and running a restore sequence by hand realistically doesn't fit inside 30 minutes — it points toward an automated or near-automated failover mechanism, like an Availability Group configured for automatic failover with a listener, or Azure SQL failover groups if this ends up as a PaaS deployment. I'd also connect this back to whatever backup strategy already exists, since RPO can never be tighter than the actual log backup frequency — if log backups currently run every 15 minutes, that's the best RPO physically achievable from backups alone, and hitting 5 minutes means either more frequent log backups or moving to continuous replication instead. I'd present the final recommendation as a direct match to the two numbers the business actually stated, so it's defensible as 'this meets what was asked for,' not 'this is generally good practice.'

exercises.title: Writing up why a database migration caused an outage, without naming who to blame
exercises.situation: A developer pushed a schema migration without running it past the DBA team first, and it caused a production outage. Explain how you'd write the postmortem.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd write that the developer caused the outage by not checking with the DBA team first, so people know what went wrong.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This names a person's shortcoming as the finding, which teaches everyone reading it the wrong lesson: the next person who makes a similar mistake now has a strong incentive to hide it rather than report it quickly. It also stops the investigation at 'a person failed to act' instead of asking what gap in the system allowed an unreviewed migration to reach production in the first place — which is the only kind of finding an action item can actually fix.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd rewrite this away from naming a person's failing and toward naming the system gap that allowed it, because a blame culture doesn't make people more careful, it makes them better at hiding problems — and DevOps specifically depends on people reporting issues fast and honestly, which a blame-first postmortem actively discourages. Instead of 'the developer pushed a migration without running it past the DBA first, causing the outage,' I'd write something like 'the migration pipeline had no required DBA review gate before a schema change could reach production, so this migration deployed without one.' That's the same underlying fact, but it points at something fixable. I'd structure the full postmortem in three parts: a timestamped timeline pulled from logs and deploy records, not memory; contributing factors — not a single root cause, but everything that let it go undetected longer, like a missing alert or a test environment that didn't match production closely enough to catch the issue first; and action items that are specific, owned, and structural — 'add a required review gate for schema migrations before production deploy' rather than 'be more careful next time.' The real test I'd apply to every sentence before it goes in the document: does it name a person's shortcoming, or does it name a gap in the system that an action item can actually close — and if it's the former, I'd rewrite it.

exercises.title: Explaining to a product manager why the Cosmos DB bill spiked after a feature launch
exercises.skillTag: Communicating Cosmos DB Cost & Throughput Tradeoffs
exercises.situation: After a new feature launched, the team's Azure Cosmos DB bill roughly doubled, and a product manager wants to know why and whether it can just be turned back down. Explain how you'd walk them through it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We're just using more of the database now, so the cost went up. We could lower the throughput setting if we want it cheaper.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Using more of the database' doesn't explain what's actually driving cost in Cosmos DB specifically, and 'lower the throughput setting' is offered without any mention of the real tradeoff — that doing so could cause the application to start getting throttled, which would turn a cost problem into an outage-shaped problem. There's no mention of Request Units at all, which is the actual unit Cosmos DB bills and throttles against.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd walk the product manager through Request Units first, since that's the actual thing Cosmos DB bills for and throttles on — every operation, a read, a write, a query, costs a specific, known number of RUs based on document size, how many properties are indexed, and query complexity, and Cosmos DB returns that exact cost on every response, so this isn't a mystery number. If we're on provisioned throughput, we're paying for a fixed, guaranteed RU/s capacity whether it's fully used or not, so the bill doubling likely means the new feature's queries are either more expensive per call — bigger documents, more complex queries with sorting or aggregation — or simply running at much higher volume than before, and I'd check which using the per-request RU charge logged for the new feature's operations specifically. I'd push back gently on 'just lower the throughput setting': if the new feature's actual RU consumption needs that higher capacity, lowering provisioned RU/s would cause 429 throttling errors under load instead of saving money cleanly, and I'd rather fix the actual cost driver than trade a billing problem for an outage. I'd offer two real options instead: if the new feature's traffic is genuinely spiky rather than steady, serverless mode could cost less since it bills only for RUs actually consumed; if it's steady but we're over-provisioned outside peak hours, autoscale would adjust RU/s automatically within a range instead of paying for peak capacity around the clock. exercises.title: Proving a query tuning fix actually worked, not just that it feels faster
exercises.skillTag: Validating a Fix with Query Store
exercises.situation: You've just applied a fix — an index change — to a regressed query. Explain how you'd prove, with evidence, that it actually worked.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd run the query again and it felt faster, so I'd call it fixed.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Felt faster' isn't evidence, isn't comparable to anything, and doesn't rule out the possibility that the query happened to run faster this one time for an unrelated reason — cached data, a quiet moment on the server. There's no baseline mentioned, no specific metric, and no tool that would let anyone else independently confirm the claim.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd prove this using Query Store rather than a subjective impression, because Query Store already has the actual historical data to compare against. Query Store keeps two related stores — the plan store, holding every distinct execution plan this query has had over time, deduplicated by query_id, and the runtime stats store, holding aggregated duration, CPU, and logical reads per plan per time interval. Before I even applied the index change, I'd have already identified this as a regressed query precisely because it showed multiple plan_id values under the same query_id with a worse-performing plan in the more recent interval — that's the actual evidence a regression happened, not a feeling that something got slower. After applying the fix, I'd query sys.query_store_runtime_stats joined through plan and query_text for this specific query_id again, and compare avg_duration, avg_cpu_time, and count_executions for the new plan against the pre-fix baseline captured in the same table. I'd also check whether SQL Server actually started using a new plan_id for this query_id post-fix, confirming the index change changed the plan at all rather than coincidentally running faster on the same plan due to something else entirely — like a quieter server at that moment. Only with that before-and-after comparison from the same data source would I report this as fixed, with actual numbers, not an impression that it felt faster this one time.

exercises.title: Declaring a SQL Server to Azure migration actually done, not just 'the data moved'
exercises.situation: A migration from on-prem SQL Server to Azure SQL Managed Instance just finished copying data. Explain what you'd check before telling anyone the migration is actually complete.
exercises.beginnerResponse: The data's all there now, so the migration is done.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'The data's all there' isn't actually verified by anything in this answer — no row count comparison, no performance check, no connectivity check — and a migration that silently dropped or duplicated rows, or that technically copied data but broke application connectivity, would pass this test while being badly broken in production.
exercises.professionalResponse: I wouldn't call this done until three specific things are confirmed, not assumed. First, row counts: I'd run the same catalog-query pattern — summing sys.partitions row counts per table, joined to sys.tables — against both source and target and diff the results table by table, since a mismatch means data was silently dropped or duplicated during the move, and that has to surface before anyone queries the new system and trusts an answer from it. Second, query performance: the same key queries that ran acceptably on-prem need to run acceptably on Managed Instance too — that's not automatically true just because the copy succeeded, so I'd compare duration and, where it matters, the execution plan, not just assume PaaS compute is equivalent. Third, and the one that catches people most often: actual application connectivity, not just confirming SSMS can connect — the real application, with its real connection string, real authentication, and real firewall path, successfully reading and writing against the new target. If something's broken post-cutover, I'd check the common failure patterns first: a connection string or firewall rule still pointing at the old server, a login that existed on-prem but wasn't recreated as a contained user on Managed Instance, since SQL logins don't migrate automatically, or a collation mismatch between source and target, which can break comparisons and joins that worked identically before in ways that are quiet and hard to spot. Only once all three checks pass would I report this as complete.

exercises.title: Deciding whether a DR plan that's 'been tested' is actually trustworthy
exercises.situation: A team says their disaster recovery plan has been tested every quarter for two years. You find out those tests were always tabletop exercises, never an actual failover. Explain what that does and doesn't prove.
exercises.beginnerResponse: If they've tested it quarterly for two years, the plan is solid.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats 'tested' as a single category, without checking which kind of test actually happened. A tabletop exercise and a real failover drill validate completely different things, and this answer can't tell leadership what residual risk still exists, because it never distinguishes between them.
exercises.professionalResponse: Two years of quarterly tabletop exercises proves something real, but not what 'the plan is solid' implies. A tabletop exercise is a walkthrough — the team talks through a disaster scenario step by step without touching production or DR systems — and it's genuinely good at surfacing gaps in the plan itself: missing roles, unclear escalation points, steps referencing a system that no longer exists. What it can't validate is whether the actual technical steps still work: whether the restore command in the runbook still runs cleanly against the current environment, or whether the failover genuinely completes inside the stated RTO. Those are only proven by an actual failover drill, which executes some or all of the recovery for real — failing over the Availability Group on purpose, or restoring a backup to a test server and verifying the data. Since this team has never run one, the real risk I'd flag is that every assumption underneath the plan's technical steps could be silently stale: the backup files might not be where the document says, the AG configuration might have drifted over two years of changes nobody updated the runbook for, and nobody would know until a real disaster forced the question. I'd recommend keeping the quarterly tabletop cadence, since it's low-cost and still useful, but adding a real drill on a longer cadence — because tabletop exercises and real drills reinforce each other; one proves the plan's logic, the other proves the commands actually still work, and claiming the plan is 'tested' on tabletop exercises alone overstates what's actually been verified.

exercises.title: Proving a MySQL performance fix actually helped, using MySQL's own tools
exercises.situation: A colleague wants to add three new indexes to a MySQL database to 'speed things up,' without having looked at anything first. Explain how you'd push back and what you'd actually do instead.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Adding indexes usually helps, so I'd just let them add the three and see what happens.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This skips measurement entirely in both directions — no check of what's actually slow before the change, and no plan for confirming anything improved afterward. It also ignores the real cost side of the tradeoff: an added index speeds up reads on that table but slows every write to it, so an unmeasured addition can trade a bigger problem for a smaller one without anyone knowing it happened.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd push back before any index gets added, because this is guessing, not tuning — the same discipline that applies to SQL Server applies here: measure before you change something, or you can't verify afterward that the change actually helped, and you risk the exact failure mode: an added index speeding up one query's reads while slowing every write to that table, trading a bigger problem for a smaller one you won't notice until later. I'd start by checking the slow query log to find out what's actually running slow on this server right now, rather than guessing which three indexes might help. For whatever surfaces there, I'd run EXPLAIN against it to see whether MySQL's optimizer is actually doing a full table scan that an index would fix, or whether the real bottleneck is something else — lock contention, insufficient buffer pool causing disk reads that should be cache hits. I'd also pull a baseline from SHOW GLOBAL STATUS and, if available, the Performance Schema, before touching anything, specifically so there's something to compare against afterward. Only then would I make one targeted change addressing the specific bottleneck EXPLAIN actually showed — not three indexes based on a hunch — and re-measure the same thing I measured first, using the same tool, to confirm the number actually moved in the right direction before calling it fixed.

exercises.title: Confirming a Cosmos DB throttling fix actually resolved the hot partition, not just the symptom
exercises.skillTag: Validating a Cosmos DB Hot Partition Fix
exercises.situation: An application was getting frequent 429 errors from Cosmos DB even though the container's overall RU consumption metric showed only 40% utilization. You suspect a hot partition and made a change to the partition key design. Explain how you'd confirm the fix actually worked.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just watch for 429 errors for a while, and if I don't see any, it's fixed.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This doesn't check the actual mechanism that was suspected — a hot partition specifically means overall metrics look fine while one physical partition is overloaded, so 'watching for errors' without checking per-partition metrics can't actually confirm whether the underlying cause was addressed or just temporarily avoided because of lower traffic.
exercises.professionalResponse: Since the original symptom — 429s with healthy-looking overall RU consumption — is the classic signature of a hot partition, I'd validate the fix the same way I'd diagnose it: by checking the Normalized RU Consumption metric sliced per physical partition in Azure Monitor, not just at the container level. Before the fix, I'd expect to have seen one partition sitting near 100% while others sat low; after the new partition key design is live, I'd confirm that same per-partition breakdown now shows traffic spread much more evenly across partitions, not just that overall utilization still looks fine, since overall utilization looked fine the whole time and never actually told us the real story. I'd also check diagnostic logs filtered to 429 responses grouped by partition key range — before the fix, those should have shown 429s concentrated on one range; after, they should either be gone or spread thin rather than concentrated. I'd specifically avoid declaring this fixed just because 429s stopped during a quiet traffic period, since the hot partition only reveals itself under real load — I'd want to confirm the fix holds during the application's actual peak traffic window, not just absence of errors during whatever window I happened to check. If the new partition key still shows any concentration, the fix isn't done — adding more RU/s would be the wrong next move, since that raises the ceiling for every partition including the ones that were never the problem, while the actual fix is getting the partition key design itself to distribute evenly.
